html:
Bussa's rebellion was the largest rising of enslaved people in the history of Barbados, in April 1816. It was named after Bussa, an African born man who led it.

The rebels believed that Britain had already freed them and that their masters were hiding it; a bill to register slaves was then being debated in London. They burned cane fields across the south and east of the island.

The militia and British troops crushed the revolt within days and hundreds of rebels were killed or executed. Yet it added to the pressure that led to the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, like the Baptist War in Jamaica. Bussa is now a National Hero of Barbados, with a statue at a roundabout outside Bridgetown.
